8138c76290a5: Eterna was founded in 1856 in Grenchen, Switzerland, by schoolteacher Dr. Josef Girard and Urs Schild, beginning life as a small movement manufacturer. The brands greatest contribution came in 1948 with the introduction of the five-ball-bearing rotor, a seemingly simple innovation that dramatically improved the efficiency and longevity of automatic movements. The design became so closely associated with the company that five balls were incorporated into the Eterna logo, and the principle has since become a standard feature of automatic watchmaking across the industry. The piece that we have here comes from Eterna's 'KonTiki' family of watches and dates to circa 1963. 309fd3dfacc3: Cabot Watch Company, better known as CWC, was founded in 1972 by Ray Mellor, a former Royal Air Force serviceman who saw an opportunity as British military watch contracts began shifting away from long-established suppliers. Named after the explorer John Cabot, the company was established with a singular purpose: to produce robust, no-nonsense timepieces built to the exacting standards of the Ministry of Defence. Where earlier names like Smiths and Newmark had defined previous generations of British-made issued watches, CWC arrived at precisely the right moment to become the standard bearer for Britain's armed forces. For the next three decades, CWC supplied everything from General Service watches to chronographs and Royal Navy dive watches, earning a reputation through reliability rather than marketing. Its asymmetrical chronographs became a familiar sight on the wrists of military personnel, while the quartz-powered G10, introduced in the early 1980s, would go on to become one of the most widely issued British military watches ever produced. Although official procurement eventually broadened beyond CWC, the company never abandoned the military-first philosophy on which it was founded, and today its watches remain remarkably faithful to the original specifications that earned them their place in British service. 014768bac0ac: CYMA’s rise to prominence was shaped by one of the most successful partnerships in early Swiss watchmaking. Founded by the Schwob brothers, the company had already established itself as a highly capable manufacturer, recognized for efficiently assembling quality watches from Swiss-made components. A pivotal moment came in 1891 when Henri Sandoz, founder of Tavannes Watch Company, relocated his operations from Le Locle to the village of Tavannes. Sandoz brought with him considerable expertise in complicated watchmaking—particularly repeaters and chronographs—complementing CYMA’s industrial organization and manufacturing strength. What began as a practical collaboration quickly proved mutually advantageous, leading to a formal merger in 1903. e8ea2089ef1f: The founding of Patek Philippe in 1839 can be traced back to the Polish insurrection of 1830. Taking part in the revolt against Russian rule was a young cavalry officer, Antoine Norbert de Patek who, like many of his compatriots was forced to flee Poland and eventually settle in Geneva. Straight away becoming involved in the city’s watchmaking industry, Patek Czapek & Co was founded with a fellow Pole, François Czapek in 1839. Then in 1844 Patek met the French watchmaker, Adrien Philippe in Paris where the latter presented his pioneering keyless winding and setting mechanism. Czapek decided to leave the company in 1845 and Adrien Philippe replaced Czapek as Patek’s partner. The company then changed its name to Patek & Cie before changing once more in 1851 to Patek Philippe & Cie. In 1932, the company was purchased by two brothers Charles and Jean Stern and since then, Patek Philippe S.A. remains a family-owned firm, with the 4th generation at its head. Today, vintage Patek Philippe is a titan in the vintage luxury watch community. Their obsessive attention to detail combined with ground-breaking feats such as the first serially produced, perpetual calendar wristwatches as well as the first split-second chronograph wristwatch, have made Patek Philippe wristwatches and pocket watches some of the most sought after in the world. a0d4841f389a: Cartier is a brand that has forever been associated with Opulence, class and sophistication. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. e0955df4bfa0: Cartier is a brand that has forever been associated with Opulence, class and sophistication. The company was founded by Louis-François Cartier in 1847 as an ‘ Atelier de Haute Joaillerie ’ after he took over the workshop of his Master, Adolphe Picard. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. Santos-Dumont complained about the difficulties of checking a pocket watch mid-flight, so Louis Cartier designed a wristwatch with a distinctive flat profile that would henceforth be known as the Cartier Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. It is considered by many to be the pioneer of modern wristwatch design. Today vintage Cartier collectors have the choice of different designs and models from London, Paris and New York houses. 6c2e51d4bed6: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, a Reference Q2601410, is a beautiful ladies' model. 33909d1cd6c6: Military watches occupy a unique place in the history of tool watches. Every detail exists for a reason. Drawing inspiration from the Bauhaus movement and its philosophy of functional, uncluttered design, Patek created what would become the archetype for the modern dress watch. Named after the Calatrava Cross—the symbol of the Spanish military order that later became the emblem of Patek Philippe—the Calatrava has served as the foundation of the manufacture's collection for nearly a century. While countless references have followed, the model's core principles of proportion, refinement, and restraint remain unchanged. This particular example, the Reference 5117G-001, dates to the 2000s and offers one of the more distinctive interpretations of the classic Calatrava formula. 126e6f4023e1: What we have here is something truly unique. Made by fine Swiss watchmaker Juvenia, this "Arithmo" calculator watch is one of the coolest watches to come across our desks. 2abedc469a11: Seiko's Tuna dive watches are known by the nicknames of "Baby Tuna," "Golden Tuna" and "Grandfather Tuna," but they could also be known as "big," "bigger," and "biggest." But rather than being big simply for the sake of it, the size of the Tunas has functionality at its heart. Seiko had released its first dive watch in 1965, the Reference 6217 (or 62-MAS). The 62-MAS was water-resistant to 150 meters and had a rotating bezel, luminous hour markers, and a 17-jewel movement (Calibre 6127) with a beat rate of 18,000. It was an excellent effort, competitively-priced compared to Swiss divers, but for Seiko, it was only the beginning. In 1968, a letter from a disgruntled professional diver in Hiroshima led to a seven year odyssey that resulted in the creation of the Tuna series of dive watches, the first ever designed specifically for saturation diving. A team of engineers led by Ikuo Tokunaga devised a circular, titanium one-piece or monocoque case with a special "L type" gasket, surrounded by a titanium shroud coated with ceramic. The crystal was held in place with a locking ring. This eliminated the need for a Helium Escape Valve, resulting in a watch that--released in 1975-looked entirely different from any dive watch that had been released. The Reference 6159-7010 was the first in a lineage of "Tuna" divers with hockeypuck aesthetics built for one purpose: never to fail. 0cf3ba424576: With a deep connection to motorsport that dates back to the Mille Miglia, it was only natural that Chopard was chosen as a sponsor and official timekeeper for the growing event. fc254811ddfd: Among the most compelling military watches of the Second World War are the RAF-issued 6B/159 navigation watches — purpose-built instruments supplied to British pilots and navigators by a select group of elite Swiss manufacturers. Produced circa 1942 at the height of WWII, this Movado 6B/159 captures the pure functionality that defined wartime aviation watches. Housed in a restrained stainless steel case measuring approximately 33mm in diameter, it wears with the elegant proportions typical of the era while retaining a strong presence on the wrist. The matte white dial features crisp black Arabic numerals, a chemin de fer minute track, and a center seconds layout designed for rapid legibility inside the cockpit. 298fc897bcad: Designing a simple watch that stands out from the pack without being outlandish is a formidable task. Indeed, most designs come up short. But not so this example from Piaget, makers of some of the world’s best ultra-thin watches: This beauty from the 1970s is that rare design that’s both rooted in the era during which it was conceived, yet forward-thinking enough to remain contemporary decades later. It features an 18K yellow gold 25mm x 28mm rectangular case with vertical, linear engraved finishing, a mineral crystal, an unsigned crown, and a crisp, mother of pearl dial framed with a black outer ring with with a minimalist "no index" aesthetic, a 'dauphine' handset, and a minimalist crown tucked into the case side. Powered by a period-appropriate quartz movement and paired to a handsome lizard skin strap with a signed yellow gold pin buckle, this incredible timepiece is suitable for most wrists and makes for a statement dress watch for the discerning collector. Horologically interesting and positively beautiful to behold, it checks all the boxes!
d2c1ddfa52db: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This particular Calatrava, a Reference 2555J, dates to circa 1950s and features a 32mm 18K yellow gold case with an acrylic crystal, an early signed crown, and a gorgeous, patinated silver dial with applied indices. Extremely minimalist and streamlined in its design language, this piece epitomizes the fundamental design details that made the Calatrava a category-defining piece upon its release. This manually wound beauty is ready for a new life on the wrist of a collector who appreciates the history of this beauty and its underappareciated appeal in the 21st century.
19c5ae216ff9: Modern dive watches tend to fall into one of two camps: those that trade on nostalgia, and those that genuinely push the category forward. The Tudor Pelagos M25600TB-0001 is firmly in the latter. While its design nods to the brand’s historic tool watches, the Pelagos was conceived from the ground up as a contemporary instrument — one that prioritizes function, durability, and thoughtful engineering over sentimentality. Executed entirely in titanium, the 42mm case is both lightweight and exceptionally robust, outfitted with a helium escape valve and rated to a formidable 500 meters of water resistance. The matte blue dial — matched to a unidirectional ceramic bezel with a luminous insert — is purpose-built for legibility, with bold square markers, an outer minute track, and the brand’s signature ‘snowflake’ handset. Everything here is designed to be read quickly, clearly, and without distraction, whether at depth or on dry land. It’s the bracelet, however, that quietly sets the Pelagos apart. Fitted with Tudor’s spring-loaded, self-adjusting clasp, it automatically compensates for changes in wrist size — whether from temperature shifts or a wetsuit compressing at depth. It’s an elegant solution to a real-world problem, and one that underscores the watch’s no-nonsense approach to utility. 7e81ea5d149b: In an era defined by exploration — of oceans, skies, and the most remote corners of the globe — watchmakers were tasked with building instruments that could keep up. Few brands embodied that spirit quite like Nivada Grenchen . By the time Admiral Richard E. Byrd returned from Operation Deep Freeze with glowing praise for the brand’s durability, its reputation had already been forged in some of the harshest conditions on Earth. What followed was a run of purpose-built tool watches that remain compelling to this day. Chief among them is the Chronomaster Aviator Sea Diver — a watch that, as its name suggests, was designed to do just about everything. Introduced in the early 1960s, it combined the functionality of a chronograph with the added utility of a rotating dive bezel, answering the growing demand for multi-purpose sports watches at a time when specialization was still taking shape. It’s a format that feels familiar now, but at the time, it was quietly forward-thinking. This particular example, dating to the 1970s and dialed 'Croton' for the U.S. market, showcases the model in one of its more refined later executions. Gone are the earlier 'broad arrow' hands, replaced here by slimmer stick hands that lend the dial a more restrained, legible quality. The overall aesthetic remains unmistakably vintage: a densely informative dial balanced by crisp sub-registers, paired with a bidirectional timing/12-hour bezel that adds both visual contrast and real utility. 03fea9f993d6: There are tourbillons that announce themselves — and then there are those, like this A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Tourbillon ref. 730.079F , that quietly assert their authority. Introduced as part of Lange’s most classically minded family, the 1815 Tourbillon is already a study in restraint, but this enamel-dial variant elevates that ethos to something approaching purity. Limited to just 100 pieces and cased in platinum, it pairs one of the brand’s most technically ambitious calibers with one of its most traditional dial-making techniques. What sets the 1815 Tourbillon apart isn’t just the presence of a one-minute tourbillon at six o’clock, but what surrounds it — or rather, what doesn’t. The dial is rendered in fired white enamel over copper, a painstaking, multi-stage process that yields a glossy, flawless surface that can’t be rushed or corrected. Large Arabic numerals, a chemin-de-fer minutes track, and blued steel hands complete the picture, punctuated by a single red “12” — a subtle nod to historic Saxon pocket watches. The result is a dial that feels at once archival and immediate, traditional yet unmistakably Lange. The model distinguishes itself not only through its rarity, but through the clarity of its execution. b77c8f3f2007: The panther holds a special place in the history of the world’s most famous jeweler. During the First World War, the Parisian maison designed a ladies’ wristwatch with a spotted diamond and onyx pattern. Commissioned by Louis Cartier, it was a gift to Belgian-French jeweler Jeanne Toussaint, whom he referred to as ‘ La Panthère .’ Over a century later, the Panthère line is still a fixture in the Cartier catalog, and the big cat motif appears frequently on watches, jewelry, and more. This particular Panthère de Cartier is a ladies’ wristwatch in the brand’s 'small' size. Housed in a 21mm two-tone case, a mineral crystal, and a stepped, smooth bezel with decorative rivets, it features an off-white dial with 'Roman numeral' indices, and a matching blued-steel ‘sword’ handset. Powered by a quartz movement and paired to a matching, two-tone multi-link bracelet, this svelte wristwatch is the very essence of Cartier: beautiful, elegant, and lasting. Whether you wear this special piece as an accent to evening wear or as an everyday watch, the Panthère in yellow gold is surely suitable.
02d1d35c9f8b: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, having designed models such as 1942’s Chronomat from the ground as a no-nonsense instrument for use in the cockpit. The Chronomat has evolved significantly since those days, retaining its aeronautical influence but greatly expanding upon its remit to include features such as dive watch-like water resistance and chronometer-grade accuracy. This particular watch, a Chronomat GMT, is inspired by models from the 1980s. Housed in a 44mm stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, screw-down pushers, and a steel timing bezel, it features a black dial with applied luminous indices, a tachymeter scale, a triple-register chronograph, a matching handset, and a handy date window at 4:30. Powered by the automatic, chronometer-certified Breitling B04 in-house movement, it comes paired to a multi-link stainless steel bracelet. Whether you’re a Breitling collector or you’re just in search for a good, old fashioned oversized chronograph, well, you've found it.
53bf6e8d2af0: Patek Philippe may be known for its complicated calendar watches, but it’s equally renowned for the simple, elegant dress watches it makes for both men and women. Take the Twenty-4 line, for example: Released in 1999, this ladies’ collection is geared toward the modern women in search of a superlative timepiece that oozes elegance and class. Available in rectangular and round case profiles in various metals and configurations, it’s one of the best dedicated women’s watch collections on the market today. This particular Twenty-4, a Reference 7300/1200A-001 , is a modern piece from the current collection. Housed in a 36mm round stainless steel case with a diamond-set bezel and a signed, screw-down crown, it features a stunning blue sunburst dial with applied, luminous 'Arabic' indices, a lumed 'sword' handset, an open outer minute track, and a date window above 6 o'clock. Powered by the automatic Caliber 324 S C, it comes paired to a matching, polished stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a fold-over clasp. Accompanied by its factory goodies and papers, this beautiful Twenty-4 is a shining example of Patek Philippe's horological bona fides. Once you take it for a spin, you're sure to be as smitten with its charms as we are!
0c23828b550a: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t often get the attention they deserve. It seems to be assumed that women are fine with shoddily designed timepieces devoid of soul. Of course, this is nonsense — there’s no reason whatsoever that a lady’s watch should be any less considered than a man’s! Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, clearly doesn't feel this way. In 1989, following the sale of his stake in the Bulgari company to his family, he established a new watchmaking firm called GB Enigma in Switzerland to design compelling timepieces with unusual designs. This particular Enigma is an exceptional piece fashioned from stainless steel. Encapsulating exactly the type of design-first mentality that Enigma took in crafting its unique pieces, it features a sapphire cabochon crown and a sapphire crystal. This piece most notably boasts an asymmetrical, almost claw-like case profile unlike anything else on the market, plus a handsome mother-of-pearl dial with a 'dauphine' handset. The red leather strap integrates directly into the case for a seamless flow tied together by a stainless steel deployant clasp, while a handy quartz movement serves as the power plant. For someone on the hunt for a design-forward timepiece to accompany an elegant night at a soirée or gala, it's an ideal choice. And did we mention it comes with its box and papers?

c39d088c64ab: Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, feels that women's sports watches should be just as compelling as men's pieces. In 1989, following the sale of his stake in the Bulgari company to his family, he established a new watchmaking firm called GB Enigma in Switzerland to design incredible timepieces with unusual designs. All told, this piece would make a great everyday watch. A lesser known brand with a powerful pedigree, an excellent design, and a practical package for everyday applications, don't let this piece slide past you! It's also a great value!
cc19b0539fa9: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, and the original Breitling Chronomat models of 1942 were built from the ground up to be no-nonsense instruments for use in the cockpit. The watch that you're looking at here is a contemporary Chronomat model that is equally no-nonsense! Dating to the 2020s, this Chronomat packs 200 meters of water resistance into the 44mm stainless steel case. Set with a polished steel bi-directional bezel, this piece possesses the classic Breitling case and bracelet paring of world renown. Its matte black dial conveys a plethora of information: An outer tachymeter scale and 1/5th-seconds track are joined by an outsized date window between 4 and 5 o'clock, applied luminous indices, and a triple-register chronograph display with running seconds, 12-hour, and 30-minute registers. A luminous 'sword' handset rounds out the feature set. Powered by the automatic Breitling B01 chronograph movement with a 70 hour power reserve, this hardy tool watch comes paired to its correct stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a signed folding clasp. Happily, it also includes its kit. In need of a serious everyday tool watch that you don't have to baby? Look no further!
8836045822e5: The Portugieser was so-called because two IWC clients from Portugal approached the manufacture with a somewhat daunting task: to produce a wristwatch that was just as accurate as a marine chronometer. In those days, the only way to ensure that degree of accuracy in a wristwatch would be to cannibalize a movement from a pocket watch and put it in a wristwatch case. The watches the resulted from such a union were large, a huge departure from the slim cases that typified wristwatches of the era. So that’s what IWC did, using a Hunter Calibre 74 pocket watch movement to create the first Portugieser. In 2015, IWC released the watch that we have here, the Reference 5102 Portuguieser made to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the original Portuguieser which debuted in 1939. This watch comes in at the same size as the original too, at 43mm wide. At the time, the standard size of most men's watches was closer to 33mm or 34mm, so while this watch isn't exactly small now, it would have been absolutely massive 75 years ago! This watch features a gorgeous matte black dial with printed 'Arabic' quadrant numerals, a subsidiary seconds counter at the 6:00 position, and an exhibition caseback, displaying the IWC Calibre 59215 hand-cranking movement with a massive 8-day power reserve. With only 750 examples made in steel, this is an excellent opportunity to pick up a contemporary classic with its full kit, and one of IWC's best releases in recent years!
4b65c5f551b3: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, comes in with a 30mm stainless steel reversible case featuring an exhibition caseback on the reverse side. The front facing dial features a classic 'Arabic' layout with subsidiary seconds and a guilloche di
e71d5d242b8a: The IWC Pilot's Watch can trace its history back to the oversized timepieces produced for military aviators in 1940. These enormous pieces were originally designed for maximum legibility in a cockpit setting, and — believe it or not — were meant to be worn on the pilot's thigh! Today, the Pilot's line is perhaps IWC's most identifiable collection, featuring a variety of case and dial configurations suited for any taste — provided your wrist can handle the larger-than-average dimensions. If not, that’s where the Mark series comes in. These watches are contemporary takes on the original Mark X and Mark XI watches from the 1940s. This particular watch, a Pilot's Watch MARK XVI, features a 39mm brushed stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a polished, stepped bezel. It houses a luminous matte black dial with printed ‘Arabic’ indices, a matching ‘sword’ handset, and IWC's Calibre 30110 with 21 jewels and a 41-hour power reserve within. Paired to a beautiful multi-link bracelet, this piece is the essence of a Pilot's watch. With excellent legibility, handsome looks, and utilitarian, military influence, it’s no surprise that the Mark series has become a cornerstone of the IWC collection.
345961d44485: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, but in the 1950's, the budding popularity of dive watches such as the Rolex Submariner and the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms pushed it to enter that race. In 1957, the brand released both a time-only dive watch, the Superocean Reference 1004, and a chronograph in the form of the Reference 807. These pieces would form the beginning of a long-lasting and ever-evolving line of nautical watches beloved by many. The watch we’re offering here is a tremendously cool, contemporary take on the Superocean that started it all. Housed in an comfortable 36mm case with a polished, white ceramic timing bezel; a signed, screw-down crown; a sapphire crystal; and a signed, blue rubber dive strap with a matching folding clasp, it's a really comfortable everyday companion to add to your collection. The luminous, blue-white dial features quadrant 'baton' markers and 'square' plots with polished surrounds as well as a stylized, luminous handset with a square-tipped seconds hand. Its attention-grabbing attribute, however, lies within a large, white chapter ring that houses a fully graduated minute track. Powered by Breitling’s COSC-certified automatic Caliber 17, this piece is accompanied by its box, travel pouch, hangtag, and card. If you’ve been on the hunt for a robust diver with some everyday appeal, then this Breitling is the answer to your prayers!
e9b3b76bc747: The Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and has in recent years once again become one of the most in-demand timepiece models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike are clamoring to get their hands on Genta's second great luxury sports watch, and with the recent news of the discontinuation of their current-collection steel, time-and-date model — the legendary Reference 5711 — this dramatic rise shows no signs of slowing down. Interestingly, most demand for Nautilus models is centered around non-complicated models, something we can't fully wrap our heads around... This particular Nautilus, a Reference 5712/1A-001 from the the 2010s , comes in with a 40mm stainless steel case with a matching integrated bracelet and signed clasp, a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a brushed bezel with polished bevels . Inside, it features a gorgeous blue gradient 'teak' dial with applied luminous indices, a power reserve indicator, a moonphase aperture with date indicator, a small seconds register, and Patek Philippe's automatic winding Calibre 240 PS IRM C LU movement beating away within. The Nautilus has become a true piece of horological history; an icon of icons; and must be experienced to be understood!
f05800904f94: Oftentimes in the hobby of watch collecting, there can be a bit too much focus on what the hot watch of the moment might be - the piece that no one can get, or the watch that everyone wants to own purely so they can say they own it. But in this frenzy of emphasis on what the next big windfall investment piece might be, there are literally tons of watches and brands which slip woefully under the radar. Tissot is among those brands. This particular Tissot is a modern beauty unlike anything else in the price category. A manually-wound skeleton, this piece has no real dial, with a complete openwork look into the industrial movement design architecture. 9eb6ac35c520: At a glance, this looks like a simple mid-century dress watch. It isn’t. This Movado Acvatic reference 18141, dating to the 1950s, deserves your full attention. Signed “Acvatic”, Movado’s period spelling for “aquatic,” this model points to its then-novel waterproof construction — and more specifically, its Borgel case. While Borgel cases are often seen in smaller, more ornate forms, finding one in a larger, round, more robust 35mm configuration like this is decidedly uncommon. A detail you might miss entirely — until you don’t. Paired with a blue leather strap, the watch balances its rugged, forward-thinking case construction with classic dress sensibility. Uncommon, quietly technical, and full of character, this is a Movado that rewards curiosity.

c8756629f6b7: The Reverso, Jaeger-LeCoultre's most distinctive watch, certainly has an impressive pedigree. One of the world's first sports watches, the Reverso combined utility with a sleek and elegant Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance an Art Deco dress watch, it owes its conception to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the 1920s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea that had taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the impact problem polo players could face on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the dial were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players risk cracking crystals or receiving damage to the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. 367a9a676417: Grand Seiko has become the darling of contemporary collectors — and it takes only a moment with one in hand to understand why. The finishing alone borders on obsessive. a066c9510531: Women’s watches have long been treated as an afterthought — reduced in size, diluted in design, and expected to sparkle their way through mediocrity. It’s a tired assumption. e06c140c12f8: There’s something quietly compelling about a watch that marks a turning point. The Movado Tempo-Matic, traces its roots to one of the brand’s most important technical milestones. 67b9315ea27b: There’s a particular kind of confidence required to make a watch this restrained. dccc48b355a6: The Space Age didn’t just put men on the moon; it reshaped design on Earth. Cars, furniture, architecture… and watches began to take on a certain orbital cool. b4ccdc3c94eb: The 1970s were not a timid decade — and neither is this Tissot. This Seastar Navigator Chronograph captures that era’s confidence in full color. 20648ae751ab: Watches have been indispensable tools for explorers since John Harrison created his marine chronometer in the 1760s, even as more sophisticated technologies like radar emerged in the 20th century. And a watch created by Jaeger-LeCoultre would be taken to the North Pole in the 1950s, on the first submarine to sail beneath the polar ice caps. But none of this could have happened without John Harrison’s chronometer; before he developed it in the 1760s, successful navigation was more a product of luck than science. The problem wasn’t latitude, but longitude. Navigators could determine their latitude by the angle of the sun at noon, or that of Polaris—the North Star—at twilight. But the rolling motion of a ship at sea rendered that method impossible when it came to determining longitude. Although scientists suggested using an accurate clock—or chronometer—for that purpose as early as the 1500s, early attempts proved insufficient when faced with the endless undulation of the ocean. This problem would prove deadly in 1707, when a fleet of four warships floundered on the rocks surrounding the Isles of Scilly. Squalls and gales had blown the ships off course, and due to the inability of the fleet’s navigators to determine their position, they assumed that they were off the coast of France. 76d907586211: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma: to simplify the perpetual calendar. 878944341bbe: There was a time when American watchmaking didn’t just compete—it led. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, a Reference Q2601410, is a beautiful ladies' model. 587572dfd48c: “Are you ready? Because I want you to pay attention. This is the beginning of something.” So opens Season 7 of AMC's Mad Men, with Sterling Cooper copywriter Freddie Rumsen pitching the new Accutron watch from Bulova. “Accutron,” he intones. “It’s not a timepiece — it’s a conversation piece . " In 1960, this thought-provoking electronic watch offered state of the art technology and design. But in order to fully understand its significance, we need to turn back the proverbial clock for a moment — all the way back to 1875. Nearly 150 years ago, Joseph Bulova established a small jewelry shop in Queens, no doubt unaware of its vast potential. In 1912, the firm opened a movement manufacture in Biel, Switzerland, carting over American mass-production methods. Within a few decades, Bulova had grown into one of the most important watchmaking manufactures in the United States. By the 1950s, progress was being made within the realm of electronic watches as an alternative to traditional mechanical watchmaking. But it was the Bulova Accutron that brought a degree of hitherto unheard-of accuracy and robustness to the scene in 1960. Its tuning fork oscillator, beating at a consistent 360 Hz, swept a seconds hand smoothly around the dial periphery, while a dry cell battery provided a constant flow of power via an electromagnetic coil. 90a6089fffaf: From the 1920s through the 1960s, small ladies’ ‘cocktail’ watches were all the rage. Fitted to a stainless steel bracelet with a deployant clasp (with original hang tags), this configuration feels solid, balanced, and ready for daily wear—less flight suit, more precision tool for modern life.

eca3437b8263: German watches are being talked about more and more recently, thanks to huge success from brands like A. Lange & Söhne and Nomos Glashutte. This particular Junghans is a rather unique chronograph, a 'Bullhead ' so-named for its rotated movement that places the pushers for the chronograph controls on the top of the case rather than the side as traditional. 34a84897a8ff: For us vintage snobs, modern Panerai can be a tricky subject. They’re either a home-run, or, well…the opposite. This beauty, the PAM00213 , is very much the former. d7b8719dfcd3: In 1968, Patek Philippe released the Golden Ellipse. Debuting eight years before the iconic Nautilus, the Ellipse — with its distinctive oval shape — was unlike anything else in Patek Philippe’s catalogs. 9f1d7dc8df8d: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. It seems to be assumed that women are fine with shoddily designed timepieces devoid of soul. 24895fe14973: One name: Gerald Genta. The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak is perhaps Genta’s most memorable work, and in many ways changed the shape of the watch industry. 5f6d7fd7690f: The history of watchmaking under the Jurgensen name goes all the way back to the 1700s to the family's progenitor, Jorgen Jurgensen, a runaway farm boy who became the apprentice to (and later, the business partner of) a heralded watchmaker in Locle, Switzerland. 8247984e2730: Here at Analog:Shift, we strive to spread the love and shine a light on lesser-known watches just as often as we extol the virtues of those built by the big brands. The El Primero was the culmination of a years-long research and development process undertaken by Zenith to develop the world’s first automatic chronograph movement. While other brands had sought to achieve the same feat — including Heuer (in concert with Breitling and Hamilton) and Seiko — Zenith intended to make the El Primero something entirely unique. Instead of taking an automatic module and merely sandwiching it onto the chronograph, Zenith fully integrated the two; moreover, the movement is a high-beat calibre offering significant added accuracy. Zenith announced the El Primero at a press conference on January 10, 1969. This was four years later than the brand had intended: the brand had begun developing the calibre in 1963, hoping to bring it out for Zenith’s centennial in 1965. Nevertheless, on that winter day in 1969, Zenith proudly displayed a working model of its chronograph. The A386 was the first model to be fitted with the El Primero movement, and therefore commands a hefty premium among collectors for its horological import. Over the past decade, Zenith has used this important model as the basis of numerous reissues, among which was a cool collaboration in honor of Land Rover's Range Rover series from 2017. The so called “Annual Calendar” bridged the gap between these two price points, offering a natural progression for collectors looking to access a Patek complication at a more accessible price point. The Annual Calendar needs adjusting just once per year. This change allows the movement to be far more economical to produce, easier to service, and cheaper to purchase. The inaugural Reference 5035 Annual Calendar of 1996 was a tremendous success, and ever since, Patek’s Annual Calendars have been a popular favorite. Eager to get into the burgeoning dive watch market, many of the best Swiss brands turned to EPSA (Ervin Piquerez, S.A.), the leading manufacturer of compressor cases at the time, for cases within which to house their divers. c1a52e4d2aa8: Despite being a relatively modern wristwatch, the IWC Aquatimer Reference 3536 has a storied history. This original model was IWC's first attempt at a dive watch, released in an era when the brand had tough competition from brands such as Rolex, Blancpain, and DOXA. At the time, IWC was known mainly for its pilot's watches, epitomized by their legendary Mark XI. Despite the developing dive watch market caused by the emergence of recreational SCUBA diving, IWC seemed resistant to enter the fray. However, the Aquatimer featured a thicker crystal and case, with patented compressor case sealing technology and a rotating inner bezel to help it withstand greater depths. c038ec63abac: Founder's Select The Reference 325 Portugieser from IWC is the first of the line — one of the very watches that spawned a collection, pushing towards a hundred years of history. Developed to satisfy the request of two Portuguese merchants who desired an oversized, highly accurate wristwatch, the 325 paired one of the International Watch Company's pocket watch movements (initially the Calibre 74) with an oversized 42mm Staybrite steel wristwatch case ("Mod. 228") produced by Biel-based Wyss & Cie. 2c4dd36aaf30: The Rolex Sea-Dweller was introduced in 1967 as the ultimate tool watch for professional saturation divers. Its development was driven by a very real challenge faced by the commercial deep-sea diving industry. During the 1960s, commercial divers working on pioneering saturation diving projects—such as France's COMEX and the U.S. Navy's SEALAB program—spent days living and working inside pressurised underwater habitats while breathing a helium-rich gas mixture known as Heliox. Because helium molecules are exceptionally small, they could penetrate the watch's rubber gaskets and accumulate inside the case. During decompression, the trapped helium expanded faster than it could escape, creating enough internal pressure to force the acrylic crystal from the watch. To solve this problem, Rolex co-developed and patented the Helium Escape Valve (HEV). Positioned at 9 o'clock on the case, this ingenious one-way valve automatically releases excess helium once the internal pressure reaches a critical level, preventing damage to the crystal and ensuring the watch remains watertight and fully functional. Offered here is the inaugural Sea-Dweller reference, the legendary ref. 1665, dating to 1979. The watch features a beautifully preserved case paired with a gently faded black bezel insert, giving it the unmistakable character collectors love to see. a9220fb9cc26: Alfred Lugrin, a highly skilled watchmaker who trained at Jaeger-LeCoultre, founded his workshop in 1884 in Switzerland’s Vallée de Joux — a region long regarded as the heart of traditional Swiss watchmaking. From the very beginning, the company specialized in producing highly complicated pocket watch movements, including repeaters, chronographs, and precision stopwatches. Between 1928 and 1930, the company officially adopted the name "Lemania Watch Co.," inspired by Lac Léman, the French name for Lake Geneva. During the economic hardships of the Great Depression, Lemania joined forces with Omega and Tissot to form the SSIH group (Société Suisse pour l’Industrie Horlogère), a move that helped secure the future of all three brands. Within the group, Lemania became the primary movement supplier to Omega, a partnership that would go on to shape some of the most important chronographs ever produced. Throughout the 1940s and 1950s, Lemania developed a series of legendary calibres, most notably the celebrated CH27 movement, later known at Omega as the Calibre 321. This movement would go on to power the Omega Speedmaster and eventually became the first and only mechanical chronograph movement flight-qualified by NASA for manned space missions. 7270c40035ef: Lanciata nel 1934, la referenza 130 è dotata di movimento Valjoux modificato al cal. 13 ed è facilmente riconoscibile per le sue anse leggermente curve e allungate e per la lunetta sottile e concava. Il modello ebbe un grande successo e rimase in produzione almeno fino al 1964. Anche se è stato prodotto per quasi 30 anni, la produzione è stata piuttosto limitata, per un totale di circa 1.500 pezzi in oro giallo, oro rosa e acciaio. Questo esemplare è una versione unica in oro giallo 18 carati, ulteriormente impreziosita da un quadrante con splendidi numeri Breguet e il nome del rivenditore “Yard” sul quadrante. Pochissimi rivenditori hanno avuto il privilegio di imprimere il proprio nome sul quadrante degli orologi Patek Philippe, rendendo il presente segnatempo ancora più esclusivo. Per quanto ne sappiamo, il presente pezzo è lunico esemplare con questa configurazione del quadrante ad essere stato immesso sul mercato! Come è normale per un orologio venduto a un rivenditore americano, “HOX” è impresso sul movimento Cal. 13CH: il codice di importazione americano per gli orologi Patek Philippe. Fibbia Patek Philippe in oro giallo 18 carati su cinturino in pelle scamosciata marrone. In condizioni originali, lossidazione dei numeri Breguet è calda e affascinante! 41bf30985b55: Lo Speedmaster nasce nel 1957. Due anni dopo, nel ’59, Omega realizzò la seconda generazione della famiglia di orologi, con lo stesso movimento della precedente – il mitico calibro 321 – ma con delle modifiche evidenti : le lancette Lollipop al posto di quelle Broad Arrow e la lunetta con la scala tachimetrica in alluminio nero e non più in acciaio. Proprio di questo modello si innamorò Walter Schirra – Wally, per gli amici – pilota della US Navy che acquistò lo Speedmaster CK 2998 in una gioielleria di Houston, qualche mese prima di partire per lo Spazio come pilota titolare della missione Mercury-Atlas 8, lanciata da Cape Canaveral il 3 ottobre 1962, a bordo della capsula Sigma 7. Durante quelle 9 ore e passa di volo, aveva al polso il suo Speedmaster. Lo aveva indossato a titolo personale, con l’intenzione di utilizzarlo come back-up per l’orologio di bordo. Anche se non fu una scelta ufficiale dell’agenzia spaziale, il CK 2998 funzionò perfettamente. Divenne così, di fatto, il primo Omega nello spazio e inaugurò la serie di esemplari utilizzati – poi su protocollo Nasa – per le esplorazioni spaziali. Questo bellissimo esemplare è in particolare una referenza 2998-3, perfettamente coevo in ogni sua componente e caratterizzato da una piacevolissima e calda patina del tempo. Completo della sua scatola originale e del suo tag! Questo è probabilmente il Rolex più iconico mai prodotto e, dato il suo breve periodo di produzione (1950 1953 circa), è oggi un modello estremamente raro e ricercato. Nel secondo dopo-guerra, verso la fine degli anni 40, lindustria orologera attraversò un periodo di forte crisi dettata soprattutto dalla difficoltà nellesportare le merci a cui conseguì una forta diminuzione del fatturato. Rolex decise di impiegare i migliori mastri orologiai nello sviluppo di nuove meccaniche sofisticate. Il design conosciuto dei vecchi Datejust e Bubbleback, forte della ormai collaudata cassa Oyster, abbracciò le nuove meccaniche su base cal. 655, per dare vita a un nuovo modello decisamente più sofisticato, con indicazione di un triplo calendario con fasi lunari, una novità assoluta per Rolex! Tuttavia, Rolex cessò presto la produzione di questa referenza, concentrandosi piuttosto sugli orologi-strumento (per lo più in acciaio) come lExplorer (1953), il Submariner (1953), il GMT (1955), ecc. Ci sono voluti più di 70 anni per rivedere un calendario con fasi lunari nella collezione Cellini contemporanea. Malgrado il fondello avvitato, limpermeabilità di questo modello era precaria ed è il motivo per cui molti quadranti si rovinarono con il passare degli anni. Ingenuamente molti di essi furono restaurati in tempi più moderni, impattando negativamente sulloriginalità e il valore
